# Takode memory

Memory is a Git repository of Markdown notes that every session can read and that Memory-phase agents keep up to date. The injected catalog is the map; the notes are the source of truth. This skill explains how the repo is organized, how to find things, how to write, and how to keep the repo healthy so the catalog stays small and useful as memory grows.

The repo lives on the Takode server's machine. Use the `memory` commands to read, search and write notes: they run on the server, so they work the same from every machine, including hosts that have no copy of the repo. Run `memory --help` for exact command syntax.

## How the repo is organized

Notes live in **topic folders at the top level of the repo**, named by subject. A topic folder holds **5 to 25 notes**, and there are no notes at the repo root. There is no limit on the number of folders; add folders as memory grows. Only when `memory lint` says the catalog is approaching its size target do you group related folders under a parent folder (see "Grouping folders when the catalog gets large"); inside a parent, each subfolder counts as one entry toward the 5-25 limit.

Every note:

- lives in exactly one folder. Never copy a note into a second folder; link to it instead.
- has a file name that is unique in the whole repo, so a moved note can always be found by name.
- starts with frontmatter:
  - `description:` one line of at most 250 characters, wrapped in double quotes, with no double quotes inside. It starts with "Read when…", "Read before…" or "Read for…" and names the concrete subjects someone would look for. It is a routing line, not a summary of findings, history or evidence.
  - `type:` one of `current` (live state or obligations that expire), `knowledge` (how something works), `procedure` (steps to do something), `decision` (an accepted choice or preference, and why), `reference` (a digest of or pointer to an outside source), `artifact` (a record of produced outputs or evidence).
  - `updated:` the date of the last substantive change. `memory commit` stamps it; commits made with `--operation repair` leave it alone.
  - `source:` a YAML list of quest IDs (`q-N`); use `session:<id>` only when no quest exists or the session itself is the durable source of truth.

Every folder has a `README.md` whose frontmatter is a single `description:` line in the same format, "Read for <subject>: <the main subtopics it holds>". It describes the folder and is not a note.

Good folder names are short subject nouns a reader would look for (`codex-recovery`, `voice`, `port-worktrees`). Do not name folders after note types (`decisions`), dates, quest IDs, or catch-alls (`misc`, `general`, `other`, `tools`).

**Repos not yet curated.** Older repos still use the six legacy type folders (`current`, `knowledge`, `procedures`, `decisions`, `references`, `artifacts`). They keep working as ordinary folders: a note there without `type:` takes its type from the folder, and a note without `updated:` uses its last Git commit date. Until a curation run reorganizes such a repo, keep putting new notes in the legacy folder that matches their type; lint's "legacy type folder" warnings are expected and are cleared by the curation run, not by ordinary upkeep.

## Reading memory

1. Start from the catalog injected into your context, or run `memory catalog show`. It has two parts:
   - **Recently updated notes**: about 50 notes in full, so you notice fresh decisions without searching. A note counts as updated when it is edited or marked helpful. `current` notes are always included; evidence (`artifact`) and `reference` notes are left out of this part.
   - **One line per top-level folder**: its note count, how many of its notes are already in the recent list, and its description. A parent folder's line also names its subfolders.
2. You may read a relevant recent note right away. **Before relying on memory for a task, list every folder whose description matches the task** with `memory catalog show <folder>`. The listing shows every note on that topic, including older notes you did not know to look for. A task that touches several topics needs several listings.
3. Read the notes in those listings that are relevant with `memory read <path>...`. Don't stop at the first note that answers the question if others also apply.
4. Use `memory grep <pattern> [<folder>...]` for exact terms, such as a file name or an error message, or when no folder description fits.
5. Use `memory catalog diff` to see which notes changed since this session last looked.
6. When a note materially helped your work, mark it: `memory helpful <path>...`. A mark counts like an update, so useful notes stay in the recent list.

**Memory handles keep outputs from repeating what you have already seen.** Every `memory catalog` output, including the injected catalog, ends with a line such as `[memory handle: mem-05de9125ba; 4 entries omitted as already shown. Pass --seen mem-05de9125ba to your next memory read.]`

- Pass the **newest** handle you have with `--seen` on your next `memory catalog` command. That output leaves out entries already shown under that handle, counts them, and gives you a new handle.
- An entry whose content changed since it was shown is always shown again.
- After a context compaction, use the handle from the catalog that arrives with the restored context, never one remembered from before the compaction.
- If you no longer have an omitted entry in your context, or you are unsure, run the command **without** `--seen` to get the full output.
- Handles you give a subagent, and handles it creates, never change yours.

## Writing memory

1. **Update before you create.** List the folder for the subject, find the existing note there (or with `memory grep`), and integrate the new facts into it. Create a note only for a genuinely new subject.
2. **Choose the folder** a future reader would open first when about to use or change this subject. When a note fits two folders, choose by what the note is about, not by which backend or tool it touches. Evidence and reference notes go in the same folder as the decision or knowledge they support. Use an existing folder whenever one fits; create a new folder only when at least 5 notes belong in it, and give it a README description.
3. **Write the description** as a "Read when/before/for…" line of at most 250 characters, using the subject words people will search for.
4. **Write the body** starting with the current answer or dated present state, its scope, material limits and genuine open questions. Integrate updates into that account and label historical or superseded material so it cannot be read as current guidance or authorization. Give detailed evidence one authoritative home and link to it, keeping the key result and caveat beside the current claim. Keep executable instructions in their authoritative instruction surface (skills, briefs, repo docs) and store only a pointer and the lesson in memory.
5. **Commit under the lock:**
   1. `memory lock acquire --owner <session-or-role>`
   2. for each note, write its full new text to a draft file and save it with `memory write <path> --file <draft>` (or `--file -` to read stdin); delete a note with `memory rm <path>` and move notes only with `memory mv`
   3. `memory lint`
   4. `memory diff`
   5. `memory commit --message "..." --source q-N --memory-id <path>` (one coherent update per commit)
   6. `memory lock release`

`memory commit` refuses a commit when a note it changes breaks a per-note rule: a description over 250 characters, a missing or unknown `type:`, a note at the repo root, or a file name used twice. Fix the note and commit again. Notes you did not change never block your commit.

## Keeping the repo healthy

After every write, run `memory lint`. It prints a summary line (notes, folders, catalog size against its target) and then errors and warnings. Fix the warnings that concern folders or notes you touched; leave everything else alone unless you are doing a curation run.

| Lint warning | Fix |
|---|---|
| folder has more than 25 entries | Split it into two or more top-level subject folders, for example `codex-recovery` and `codex-launch-config` instead of one `codex`. |
| folder has fewer than 5 entries | Merge it into the closest related subject folder. Never create a catch-all just to reach 5. |
| folder has no README description | Write `README.md` with a one-line `description:`. |
| description over 250 characters, or not a "Read when/before/for…" line | Rewrite it as a routing line and move any detail into the body. |
| legacy type folder | Cleared by a curation run (below). |
| reference to a missing memory note | Point the link or mention at the note's current path. |
| current note not updated in 30 days | Refresh it, or remove it if the state no longer applies. |
| catalog past its size warning | See "Grouping folders when the catalog gets large". |

Move notes only with `memory mv <old> <new>`, or for many notes `memory mv --plan <file>` (one `old new` pair per line). It creates missing folders, moves the files, rewrites every reference to them in other notes (Markdown links, absolute paths and plain or inline-code mentions alike), fills in a missing `type:` and `updated:`, and keeps helpful marks.

Commit moves, README edits and description rewrites with `memory commit --operation repair`. A repair doesn't change what notes say, so it does not stamp `updated:` (notes don't jump into the recent list) and the notes it touches are not held to the per-note rules.

## Reorganizing a repo (curation run)

Use this when lint shows structure warnings across the repo (for example legacy type folders after the upgrade to topic folders), or when asked to curate memory. A repo of a few hundred notes takes one agent roughly 5-10 minutes plus description rewrites. Memory is durable user data: work under the lock, keep every note, and change only frontmatter descriptions, READMEs and references, never note bodies' substance.

1. **Back up first.** On the Takode server's machine, copy the whole repo directory, including `.git`, to a dated backup location outside the repo (for example `tar -czf <backup-dir>/memory-<space>-<date>.tgz -C "$(dirname "$(memory repo path)")" "$(basename "$(memory repo path)")"`) and record its path and checksum in your quest notes.
2. Take the lock and run `memory lint` to see the warnings and the current catalog size.
3. Run `memory catalog show --all` to see every note with its description. Reuse folders that already fit. On older notes, `facets: topic:` lists in the frontmatter are useful grouping hints.
4. Group notes by **subject**, meaning what a future reader would be looking for, not by note type or date:
   - aim for 10-20 notes per folder; 5-25 is the hard range;
   - a subject with more than 25 notes becomes several sibling folders with a shared name prefix (`codex-recovery`, `codex-launch-config`);
   - a subject with fewer than 5 notes joins the closest related folder;
   - put each note where a reader would look first; evidence and reference notes go with the decision or knowledge they support.
5. Write all moves into one plan file and apply them with `memory mv --plan <file>`. Keep file names unchanged.
6. Write a `README.md` description for every new folder.
7. Rewrite every description in the touched folders that is not a "Read when/before/for…" routing line, or that is over 250 characters. When the old description summarizes findings, read the top of the body so the new line stays accurate.
8. Run `memory lint` until it shows no errors and no structure warnings: no legacy type folders, every folder within 5-25 entries with a README description, no references to missing notes. Then `memory commit --operation repair` (more than one commit is fine) and release the lock.
9. Check the result: `memory catalog show` should list the recent notes and one line per topic folder, and a couple of folder listings should read sensibly.

A large repo may be reorganized in several runs, one group of folders at a time. Every run must leave lint clean for the folders it touched.

## Grouping folders when the catalog gets large

The injected catalog has a size target of about 16k tokens. The recent list is a fixed ~3k tokens; the folder lines grow with the repo. Lint warns when the catalog passes about 12k tokens (48,000 characters), which with top-level folders alone happens at roughly 1,500-3,500 notes. Act in this order:

1. **Merge small related folders** toward 20-25 notes each. This removes catalog lines without hiding anything.
2. **If the catalog is still too large, group related top-level folders under a parent**, for example `codex/recovery`, `codex/launch-config` and `codex/subagents` under `codex/`. Use the same `memory mv --plan` flow. The parent's README describes the whole group, and the parent holds 5-25 entries in total, counting each subfolder as one entry. The catalog shows one line for the parent naming its subfolders; listing the parent shows each subfolder's description. Group only as much as needed to get back under the warning.
